questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My main concern was going somewhere that had mountains and outdoor activities which Bozeman definitely fulfills. Besides that, I also wanted to go somewhere with interesting culture and getting away from the coasts in the US, you get that. Finally, I also wanted to make sure I was able to take some classes that would benefit me academically and some just for fun.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I might be a little biased, especially since I've traveled a lot in the States before and swung by Bozeman but I really enjoyed myself.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, most if not all was given to you in advance and if not, the office of incoming exchange students was really fast with replying to emails, within a day.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I went to a few orientation events. Didn't need the airport pickup though that was avaiable.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: You could definitely get more assistance than I got if you needed it or simply wanted it, very helpful and involved staff.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Many different dorms with some student apartments though it was my impression that these were mainly for graduate students. Some dorms were equipped with more ammenities like ski rooms, a shared kitchen, a gym, and a variety of different common areas though of course these were also more expensive.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Three different meal plans ranging from 5 - 7 days a week and the dining halls did have a pretty impressive selection if not always the most flavorful or vegetarian friendly. Most dorms would have a small kitchen for everyone to share but it would have very little stuff, most of which you would have to check out at the reception to use like pots and pans so not very easy to make your own food.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It's definitely a little expensive and it can feel limiting sharing a room all of a sudden (though single rooms are available), checking in after 10 PM, etc. but it was a great way to meet a lot of new people easily and make friends which is pretty nice as a new-to-town exchange student who doesn't know.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Generally, not a nice long-term solution if you're staying for two semesters but I really enjoyed staying there for one.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If a class is already filled up, it's possible to write to the professor of the course directly and they might make an exception for you as an exchange student and let you in anyway.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You can read about the different courses on the MSU website and for the actual registration, you do it through an online portal which generates a schedule for you so you can see if any courses clash with each other. Not too difficult to register.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Again, the office of incoming students was pretty fast with replying to emails.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into all the classes I wanted, including two graduate courses (even though I'm an undergrad) and a class which was filled up but after writing the professor, I got in anyway.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: WRITE the professor if you want a spot in a filled class, they might say no but most likely they'll say yes if you argue your case.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I kinda went on both sides of the spectrum: I took two second-year courses (Creative Writing and Great Books) open for everyone which were pretty easy to pass as long as you did the homework which in these courses weren't too excessive, a little time-consuming certain times but never hard to complete. On the other hand, I took two physics graduate courses (I'm a physics student) which were very difficult, weekly assignments to turn in as part of your final great and decently high level. Genereally, I would say the level depend a lot on the specific course though maybe a senior course (400-code) would fit for most fifth-semester bachelor students from KU.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Less classes and readings and more homework and due assignments. Only lectures in my physics classes, no time specificly to solve problems so you're kinda alone with your assignments. You can (and are supposed to) go to your professor's office hours and ask questions but that still wasn't optimal, I definitely struggled with my physics courses and missed the way we do it at KU.
My liberal arts classes were not as bad and the creative writing class was actually a workshop resulting in more varied classes.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PHYS 501 Advanced Classical Mechanics
PHYS 544 Condensed Matter Physics I 
LIT 203IH Great Books
CRWR 240RA Introduction to Creative Writing

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Advanced Classical Mechanics for physics students, intense but level not too difficult as a third-year.

Creative writing for everyone (Molly Damm as instructor for poetry-workshop). It was such a fun, creative, comforting and safe space, only 20 people in the class, many of whom said that the course were the highlight of their week (I felt that too).

Great Books was also really fun, kinda like a big bookclub and the professor was really charismatic, smart and fun, highly recommend.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
The dollar was pretty high when I had to pay for accommodation (7.5 DKK = 1 USD).
Bozeman in general is pretty expensive, grocery-wise and eating out.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Busses were free, splitting gas with friends is cheap. 
Coffee is pretty cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In the US, you can satisfy most hobbies and interests through schools and universities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: So many different things to do! Mostly outdoorsy adventure stuff but also debate, frisbee, bowling, choir, music, and much more.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed various outdoor clubs for outdoor activities. Backcountry squatters (if you're a girl or non-binary) and the outdoor club (everyone).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
On weekends, everyone leaves campus to go hiking or backpacking in the mountains which I highly recommend, so much nature nearby and national parks not too far away.
For longer holidays, renting a car and going on a small roadtrip is a lot of fun.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, no language barrier and the culture is not too foreign.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
The drinking culture is less emphasized (though still exist) than in Denmark so doing stuff that doesn't involve drinking is pretty common. 
Joining clubs is a great way to make friends, more common than meeting people in class probably.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Some people are more conservative and religious which you just have to remember sometimes before making a joke. Politics could be a more sensitive topic than in Denmark.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Americans are just some of the kindest and most helpful people I've ever met. Some of the small talk might seem superficial but if you make it through that, many times it can lead to actual friendships or help.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Keep your weekends sacred for going on adventures.
2. Take fun, random classes if you have the electives to do so!
3. Smuggle food out of the dining halls during the week if you have the 5-day meal plan. That way you'll have some food for the weekends and save on groceries.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Having a car available in some way was pretty essential for doing stuff on the weekends. My friends and I didn't buy one because even used cars had gotten quite expensive so we made friends with people who had cars instead.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
It might be cliche but the amazing people I met: internationals from Europe and elsewhere, nationals from other states and local Montanans. 
And I really loved being that close to the mountains with so many outdoor activities easily available.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Taking graduate courses while wanting to have fun and enjoy my time as an exchange student.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Remember to have fun!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
